[lead] PAYSON — Hail, wayfarer, and a bright good morning to you, under a clear sky and a kind sun over the pines! Today the Hold offers a farmers market in Sedona, a thoughtful discussion circle here in Payson, the last hours of a river retreat in Camp Verde, and live music in Prescott. The days ahead bring an open mic in Pine, a trail-building morning, and Halloween doings on Saturday, Oct. 31 — by the Nine, a merry week for every traveler on the Rim road.

[today Payson] Spiritual Soup — a monthly discussion group that meets on the 2nd and 4th Sundays, today from 11:15 AM to 12:15 PM at 904 N Beeline Hwy, Suite E, and on Zoom. Today’s topic is “Forgiving Yourself and Others — What Is Your Experience?”, led by facilitator Teri Taylor. Each person may bring a thought to share, or simply listen in good company. A love offering is taken. A gentle, friendly way to spend a Sunday hour.

[today Camp Verde] A Sanctuary for your Soul Retreat at the River House — the last morning of a full-moon retreat weekend that began Friday, Oct. 23, ending today at 12:00 PM in Camp Verde. Guests have spent the weekend on morning yoga and breathwork, sound healing, quiet time by the river, and rest in nature. If a slow, restoring weekend sounds like your kind of quest, this is the one travelers have been talking about. Space on these weekends is limited, so plan ahead for the next one.

[today Sedona] Sedona Community Farmers Market — winter hours today from 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM in the Wells Fargo Bank parking lot at 2201 W SR 89A in West Sedona. Look for local and regional harvest goods and artisan products, with live music from Tobie LaVoie and Friends while you browse. Pastured chicken, grass-fed beef, artisan breads, honey, and farm eggs are among the regular offerings. A fine Sunday outing under the red rocks, and worth the drive down the Rim.

[today Prescott] Tone Kings — Live at Whiskey River Tavern — live music today at 1:00 PM at 214 S. Montezuma St in Prescott. Settle in at a Whiskey Row tavern for an afternoon set, the kind of mead-hall hour a bard would approve of. Good tunes, good company, and a town square worth a stroll before or after the show. Valley Dwellers up for the cool air will find Prescott in fine form today.

[week Mon, Oct. 26] Open Mic Night: Music with a Purpose — THAT Brewery & Pub, 3270 AZ-87 in Pine, 4:00–7:00 PM. Singers, players, poets, and storytellers are all welcome, hosted by rotating members of the Fuel Reduction team, with tips benefiting Fuel Reduction. Cheer on your neighbors over a pint in the pines. | Olive Oil Tasting — Sedona — 4:00 PM at 336 Arizona 179, Suite C102, Sedona. A tasting outing for cooks and gift-hunters alike; come ready to compare flavors and learn what makes a good oil sing.

[week Tue, Oct. 27] Trail Day Volunteer Build — Pine — 7:00 AM to 12:00 PM off Highway 87 just before Pine. Volunteers clear brush, move rocks, and shape a trail that will serve hikers, bikers, and runners for years, and help fire crews reach the forest when it counts. Tools are provided; bring water, sunscreen, gloves, and sturdy shoes. No experience needed — email trails@psfuelreduction.org for directions. | Youth Art Class — Show Low — 11:00 AM at 100 N White Mountain Rd, Suite 101, Show Low. A class morning for young artists; register through Kittles Fine Art under “Upcoming Classes.”

[week Wed, Oct. 28] Bible Study at Juanita’s — Payson — 9:00 AM at 139 Hash Knife Drive in Payson. A small, friendly morning gathering around the table; newcomers are welcome to pull up a chair. | High Altitude Baking Workshop — Prescott — 5:00 PM at 840 Rodeo Dr, Building C, Prescott. Baking at mountain height is its own small magic — cakes rise differently up here — and this workshop is the place to learn its secrets. | Musicians with Heart Open Mic — Prescott — 7:00 PM at the Jersey Lilly Saloon in Prescott. An evening open mic on Whiskey Row, where local players take their turn and the room listens kindly.

[week Thu, Oct. 29] Windmill Park Farmers Market — Cornville — 2:00 PM at 9950 E Cornville Rd in Cornville, in the Verde Valley below Camp Verde. A weekday market stop for farm goods and local wares on a pleasant autumn afternoon.

[week Sat, Oct. 31] Show Low Main Street Halloween Trunk or Treat — 3:00–8:00 PM at Hatch Toyota, 1051 N Auto Mall Pkwy, Show Low. The setting is a cooking contest semi-final, and the audience helps choose who goes on to the finals — supper and sleuthing in one.

[merchant name] Pioneer Village Trading Post

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] A treasure-hunter’s trading post on the north end of the Beeline, stocked by many hands over many years — rooms stacked high with vintage home décor, collectibles, pottery, glassware, and a large selection of antique American Indian jewelry, as Visit Arizona tells it. By some small enchantment of the Hold, every visit turns up something nobody remembers putting there — that is the fun of the place. Go in for one thing, hail traveler, and come out carrying three.

[merchant review] Pickers praise the wandering most of all — room after room of vintage décor, collectibles, and antique jewelry, with the fun lying in what turns up next.

[merchant review_src] Visit Arizona — Payson Pit Stops

[tale title] The Great Acorn Necklace Parade

[tale] Sundas dawned warm and golden, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) announced a parade. Not for any reason, mind — the acorns were falling, the sun was out, and that dang ol’ Jethro has never once let a good morning go uncelebrated.

All morning he sat in the clearing stringing fallen acorns onto twine, making necklace after necklace. Earl (an elk) received the longest one and wore it with enormous dignity, holding his head high so it would not slide down his neck. Henny (the Hearth’s plump chicken) refused a necklace outright, climbed onto the biggest pumpkin by the porch instead, and led the whole parade from up there like a queen on a very round throne.

Round the clearing they went, three times, Jethro waving at nobody, Earl stepping slow and stately, Henny clucking the beat. Mabel sighed, said it was the finest parade the Hold had seen all week, and went back to her garden. She was not wrong.

[tale image caption] Henny leads the parade from the finest seat in the Hold.

[today Payson] Monster Mash, 4:00 to 9:30 p.m. in Payson. Payson’s big family Halloween evening starts earlier this year so families have more room to come and go across the night, with costumes, crowds, and a fall evening outdoors. Bring chairs and blankets for the outdoor Halloween movie, The Nightmare Before Christmas, and enjoy the fun as Valley Dwellers trade the lowland heat for Rim Country air. Expect a long, festive evening rather than a quick trick-or-treat stop, so check Adventure Payson for the venue details before you go. | Payson Public Library 2026 Book Sale — final day, 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. at Payson Public Library, 328 N. Today is the last chance, so come with a tote bag and leave with winter reading. It is an easy, unhurried stop for guests who like a rummage with a purpose. | Truckload Meat Sale at Tractor Supply, 9:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. in the parking lot at Tractor Supply, 510 SR-260, Payson, on its second and final day. The tent advertises 20 ribeyes for $50, family packs of beef, chicken, seafood, and pork, and discounts for first responders, military, and seniors on most packs, with cash, cards, and EBT accepted. It is a stock-the-freezer stop, not a festival — go early in the day for the widest pick. Ask at the tent about the day’s specials before you buy.

[today Camp Verde] Breast Cancer Awareness Walk, 7:00 to 9:00 a.m. at Middle Verde Heritage Park in Camp Verde, with a second walk site at the Clarkdale Learning Center. The Yavapai-Apache Nation’s CHR/WIC and Diabetes Program invites YAN community members to walk together this morning, with giveaways for participants. It is an early, good-hearted start to the day, made for community members rather than drop-in visitors. Questions go to the program contacts named on the Nation’s page. | Camp Carpe Diem Verde Valley 2026, running October 22–25 at Verde River RV Resort & Cottages, 1472 West Horseshoe Bend Drive, Camp Verde. This hosted RV-and-camping weekend uses Camp Verde as its base for exploring the whole Verde Valley, with hiking, biking, breweries, wineries, and ghost towns by day and campfire gatherings by night. It is a social, ticketed gathering rather than a drop-in town fair, so guests already in the valley with an RV will get the most from it. Expect a ready-made company of fellow travelers and a planned menu of outings.

[today Sedona] Fall Arts & Crafts Fair, 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. at the Sedona Heritage Museum, 735 Jordan Road, Sedona. The museum’s annual fall fair is timed for early holiday shopping, with handmade jewelry, ceramics, fine art, home décor, cards, woodcarvings, glass, candles, and lotions from local and regional makers, and lunch available for purchase. Many of these artisans do only this show or a handful of others, so the goods are genuinely hard to find elsewhere. The museum grounds in Jordan Historical Park make it a pleasant browse, not a mall run. | Sedona Plein Air Festival — Finale and Final Art Sale, 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. at the Sedona Arts Center, 15 Art Barn Road, Sedona, with free admission per the festival guide. After a week of artists painting the red rocks outdoors, the festival closes with a community paint-out in the morning, judging at noon, and the final art sale from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. There is even pumpkin painting by the festival artists from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. It is the last chance to meet the painters and buy the week’s work before they leave town.

[today Prescott] Prescott Centennial AirFest, 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. at Prescott Regional Airport — Ernest A. Love Field, 6110 Wilkinson Drive, Prescott, and free per the City page. The airport celebrates its centennial with aircraft and military displays, food trucks, and a Touch-a-Truck with Prescott Fire and Copperstate Ambulance so kids can climb on real equipment. It is an open-air, wander-at-your-own-pace day rather than a seated airshow. A good all-ages outing, and an easy drive for guests already headed to Prescott. | Costumes for Kids 5K & Halloween Fest, starting 9:00 a.m. in Prescott, per the Prescott Places weekend picks. Runners and walkers take the course in costume for a Halloween-morning fundraiser feel — part race, part costume parade, and friendly to families. Expect a merry crowd in the cool morning air rather than a serious race-day scrum. Check the weekend listing for the start place and sign-up details before you go.

[week Sun, Oct. 25] Prescott — Prescott Community Gardens Fall Festival, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. at the Prescott Community Gardens, per the Prescott events calendar; the listing did not print the street address, so check it before you go. The gardeners open the gates for a fall celebration among the beds — a harvest-season gathering with the year’s growing behind it and winter planting ahead. Expect neighbors, garden talk, and a last wander through green things before the frosts settle in. A gentle Sundas outing for guests who garden, or wish they did. | Sedona — Haunted History, 3:00 to 4:00 p.m. at the Sedona Heritage Museum, 735 Jordan Road, Sedona, with tickets at $10 per the museum calendar. An hour of Sedona’s spookier local history, told at the museum in Jordan Historical Park — ghost-season storytelling with real town stories behind it. It is a seated, small-room kind of outing, good for guests who like their Halloween with a history lesson. Arrive a little early, for museum programs fill their chairs fast. | Payson — Spiritual Soup, 11:15 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. at 904 N. Beeline Highway, Suite E, Payson, and on Zoom. This monthly discussion group takes up a spiritual topic together — this meeting’s topic is Forgiving Yourself and Others — with a facilitator and a love-offering basis. It meets on the second and fourth Sundays, so this is the month’s second gathering. A quiet, thoughtful hour for guests who like conversation over coffee-table topics.

[week Mon, Oct. 26] Pine-Strawberry — Open Mic Night: Music with a Purpose, 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. at THAT Brewery & Pub, 3270 AZ-87, Pine. Local players, singers, poets, and storytellers take turns rather than one headline act, hosted by members of the Pine Strawberry Fuel Reduction team, with tips benefiting Fuel Reduction’s work. Open mics in the twin villages are community living rooms — expect neighbors, a few surprises, and music made for love of it. It is good for guests who want an evening that feels like the town, not a show put on for tourists. | Sedona — Verde Valley Fiber Artisans, 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. at the Sedona Heritage Museum, 735 Jordan Road, Sedona, per the museum calendar. Fiber artists gather to work, talk shop, and share projects in the museum’s setting — weaving, spinning, and stitching among people who love the crafts. Visitors who sew, knit, or weave will find kindred spirits and plenty to look at. Check the museum calendar before you go for the room and any supply notes.

[week Tue, Oct. 27] Pine-Strawberry — Trail Day Volunteer Build, 7:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. on the trail project off Highway 87, just before Pine. Pine Strawberry Fuel Reduction calls hikers, bikers, runners, and neighbors to help clear brush, move rocks, and shape a trail that will also give firefighters better access when the community needs it. Tools are provided, no experience is needed, and volunteers bring water, sunscreen, gloves if they have them, and sturdy shoes. To volunteer, email trails@psfuelreduction.org and the directions and details come back by return mail.

[week Thu, Oct. 29] Pine-Strawberry — Haunted Barn at the Pine Community Center, 5:00 to 10:00 p.m. at the Pine Community Center grounds, 3886 AZ-87, Pine. The twin villages raise their haunted barn for Halloween week — a walk-through fright made by locals, in a real barn, under the Rim. It is the Holdings’ own harvest-of-scares, merry and spooky in equal measure, and a fine excuse for an evening drive up the 87. Check the event page for tickets and age guidance before you go, and mind the mountain road home. | Sedona — Fiddler on the Rock, 5:15 to 6:45 p.m., listed on the Sedona Heritage Museum calendar; the listing did not name the exact room, so check it before you go. A fiddler plays among the red rocks in the late light — a small, musical evening rather than a big concert-hall night. It pairs well with a slow Uptown supper afterwards. Guests who love a tune with their sunset will be glad they went.

[merchant name] Old County Inn

[merchant town] Pine

[merchant blurb] In a stoplight-free mountain town under the Rim, Old County Inn fires up its wood oven every day it is open for scratch-made wood-fired pizzas, with the sausage, bacon, pickles, and cocktail syrups all made in house. By the Nine, a pizza oven that good would need a little magic in Skyrim, so picture a neat heat enchantment roaring behind the counter while the famous Meat Pie and the creamy Burrata pizza come out generous and hot. The signature thing to try is the Burrata pizza — and the Green Chile Beer Cheese with breadsticks while you wait.

[merchant review] This little Pine, Arizona Inn truly has some of the best and most creative woodfired pizzas we’ve had anywhere.

[merchant review_src] TripAdvisor review

[merchant why] Because it is Rim Country’s own scratch-made pizza hall — wood-fired pies, Arizona craft beer, and a meadow under the pines, twenty minutes up the road in Pine. Great praise is great, and this little inn has earned every word!

[merchant visit] 3502 N. Highway 87, Pine, AZ 85544. Hours: Wednesday–Sunday 11:00 a.m.–9:00 p.m., closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Phone: (928) 476-6560. Price range: moderate ($$). [tale title] The Great Monster Mash Costume Fitting

[tale] Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) woke under a partly cloudy Loredas sky with a grand notion: Earl (an elk) should go to tonight’s Monster Mash in costume, and Jethro would fit him himself. Out came pine boughs, a coil of twine, and a hollow pumpkin saved for just such an emergency.

Earl stood very still and very dignified while Jethro tied boughs along his back like a forest come to life. The pumpkin hat, though, would not sit straight between those enormous antlers — left, right, left again, until it settled at a jaunty angle that Jethro declared ‘terrifying, probably.’ Henny (the Hearth’s chicken) walked one slow circle as judge, pecked the twine once, and gave a single approving cluck.

Then a butterfly crossed the clearing, Earl turned his head to watch it, and the whole costume turned with him — boughs, pumpkin, and all — like a small woodland revolving door. Jethro clapped anyway. If you see a pine forest dancing at the Mash tonight, traveler, that is not a forest. That is Earl, and he would like you to know he is a monster now.

[tale image caption] Earl’s Monster Mash fitting — boughs, pumpkin, and one approving cluck.

[tale title] Earl’s Rainy-Day Walk

[tale] Earl (an elk) takes his daily walk at the same hour every day, storm or shine, and a little thing like a Turdas downpour was not going to move him. So when the rain came hammering down, Earl stepped out with his chin high and his antlers proud, exactly as planned.

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) could not stand the sight. He tore a pine bough the size of a barn door off the windfall pile and trotted along beside Earl, holding it over them both like a walking roof. Henny (the Hearth’s chicken), who had no intention of getting wet either, fluttered up and rode dry between Earl’s antlers, looking very pleased with her arrangements.

Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) tried to help by chilling the raindrops over Earl’s head, and succeeded only in giving him a hat of small, tinkling hail. Earl endured the whole parade — the bough, the chicken, the hail hat — with perfect dignity, finished his walk at the usual fence post, and shook himself like a great wet dog all over Jethro. Mabel (a wood elf) watched from the porch and said it was the finest roof she had ever seen walk.

[tale title] The Puddle Mirror Fair

[tale] The storms rolled over the Rim all Middas morning, and by noon the Hearth clearing was a shining quilt of rain puddles. Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) had an idea, as Flurry does: one careful, frosty breath across each puddle, and every puddle turned into a perfect little mirror.

[tale] Morndas dawned grey and drippy, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) announced that the low cloud over the Hearth was far too good to waste. He fetched a row of Mabel’s canning jars and set about catching the fog to water her garden later, one jar at a time, waving each lid like a butterfly net.

[tale title] The Pancake That Would Not Land

[tale] Sundas dawned drizzly, and Gus (an orc baker) marked it the only proper way: one enormous pumpkin pancake on the Hearth deck, wide as a cartwheel, flipped high enough to need a witness. Mabel (a wood elf) appointed herself witness, mostly to say she had warned him.

The flip was perfect. The landing was not. A gust off the Rim took the pancake sideways, and Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) zigzagged after it with a tray, tail kink and all, while Henny (the Hearth’s chicken) ran the deck below like a one-bird ground crew.

That dang pancake sailed clean over the tray, over Henny, and settled — soft as you please — square on Earl’s antlers, where it sat like a grand golden beret. Earl (an elk) stood very still, wearing his breakfast with complete dignity, and declared it the finest hat in the Hold. Gus agreed, and served the next one on a plate, like a coward.

[today Payson] Payson Drive ’n Dine to Crosswinds Restaurant — cars leave Mesa at 9 AM and reach Payson before 10:30 AM for breakfast and lunch at Crosswinds, by Payson Airport. The Audi Club of Arizona’s mountain run up the Beeline ends where model planes hang from the ceiling and real ones sit outside the windows. The listing invites non-members to take a test drive with the club, and non-Audi cars are welcome too. Watch for the caravan rolling into town mid-morning. | Morning Café — Unity of Payson — 9:30 AM–12:30 PM, 110 E Bonita, Payson, and on Zoom every Saturday. A gentle, coffee-hour start to Loredas: good company and an uplifting talk to open the day. It runs every Saturday, so guests can join from the Hearth by Zoom without driving anywhere. Check unityofpayson.org for the blue Zoom link.

[today Camp Verde] Beaver Creek School Reunion — from 9 AM, Beaver Creek School, Beaver Creek School Rd, Rimrock, just south of Camp Verde. A full day of reconnecting and reminiscing for the school’s friends and faculty, with a Flag Assembly at 10 AM, an assembly at 11 AM, lunch at noon, and activities into the afternoon. A true small-school homecoming — old classmates, old teachers, and stories from the Beaver Creek valley. The listing asks folks to register ahead of time. | The Blue Canyon Band Residency — 8 PM–midnight, Cliff Castle Casino and Hotel, Camp Verde. Two nights of live band music close out the week, and tonight is the second show of the band’s weekend residency. Expect a party crowd, dancing energy, and casino-hall entertainment right off I-17. The popular Starlight run rides four hours through Verde Canyon — daylight first, then sunset colour on the cliff walls, then twilight and starlight under wide skies. Romantic, unhurried, and one of the Verde Valley’s signature evenings. These Saturday trips run on select Saturdays through Nov. 21.

[today Sedona] Fest of Fall — 12–6 PM, Posse Grounds Park, 525 Posse Ground Rd, Sedona. The City of Sedona’s big fall party packs food trucks, craft and community vendors, a Kids’ Zone, a Gaming Center, and a Ride Jam at the skate park into one afternoon, with pickleball and cornhole tournaments and live music all day. Halloween starts in a swimming pool: families jump in to pick their very own floating pumpkin from the water. After the splash, kids decorate their pumpkin at a no-mess sticker station and take home a goodie bag. Registration secures a pumpkin and a raffle ticket. Today’s programme adds workshops on screenwriting, music in film, and learning to pitch, alongside film blocks through the day. Sunday closes with a free showcase block.

[today Prescott] Taiko Drumming Workshop and Taiko Extravaganza — workshops 9 AM–1 PM and evening show 7 PM, Elks Performing Arts Center, 117 E Gurley St, Prescott. World-class taiko artist Ken Koshio leads a beginner-friendly, hands-on workshop in ancient Japanese drumming — all drums provided, no experience needed. The day crescendos with the evening Taiko Extravaganza, fusing Japanese drumming and world music with World Hoop Dance Champion Derrick Suwaima Davis. Taiko is heard with the whole body — feel it in your chest. | OktoberMarket with Holly Ridge — 12–8 PM, The Grand Highland Hotel, 154 S Montezuma St, Prescott. Prescott’s fall market season kicks off inside the hotel ballroom and out in its courtyard, with artisan vendors offering organic skincare, baked goods, jewellery, apparel, woodwork, and soaps. There are pumpkins and spooky treats for kids and kids at heart. Come for coffee, stay for lunch, or wander in after dinner — this year they are testing longer hours. | Free Garden Class: Effortless Plants for Busy Gardeners — 9:30–10:30 AM, 1815 W Iron Springs Rd, Prescott. Want a gorgeous garden without spending every weekend on upkeep? This free morning class dives into low-maintenance plants that actually thrive in the Arizona climate. Expect practical picks and care tips aimed at busy gardeners who would rather relax in their yard than labour in it. Arrive curious; leave with a planting list.

[week Sun, Oct. 18] Howl-O-Ween Dog Costume Parade — 10 AM–noon, check-in 9–9:30 AM, Tlaquepaque Arts & Shopping Village, Sedona; registration $20, benefiting the Humane Society of Sedona. Costumed canines parade through the courtyards for $100 prizes as Doggone Cutest, Craziest Canine, and Leaders of the Pack, with a 50/50 raffle and swag bags besides. Dress up your dog, yourself, or the whole family. Spectators line the route — pure Sedona charm with wagging tails. | Sedona Community Farmers Market — winter hours — 11 AM–3 PM, Wells Fargo Bank parking lot, 2201 W State Route 89A, West Sedona. The market settles into its Sunday winter hours with live music and vendors offering pastured chicken, grass-fed beef, artisan bakery goods, fish, honey, eggs, and pot pies. Seasonal produce, specialty foods, and handmade crafts fill out the stalls. Leashed, well-behaved dogs are welcome. A slow Sunday browse under the red rocks.

Watch festival artists paint across the ranch grounds from 4–6 PM, among the historic red barn, pastures, ponds, orchards, and vineyards. Awards and an exclusive sale of the works created that very afternoon follow at 6:30 PM. D.A. Ranch wines are for sale, with a grazing table and live music. Golden-hour art, wine, and music in the Verde Valley.

The work also creates better access routes for firefighters and emergency crews. Tools are provided; bring water, sunscreen, gloves if you have them, and sturdy shoes. Email trails@psfuelreduction.org for directions.

The Plein Air Festival’s most intimate evening: a small audience watches artists paint from 4–6 PM amid sweeping red-rock views. A grown-up camp and “UnRally” for RVers, van-lifers, tent campers, and travellers: four days exploring the valley’s hiking, biking, breweries, wineries, and ghost towns. Organisers handle the details; campers pick how much or how little to do, with community dinners along the way. This year’s edition lands at peak fall colour. Come for the adventure; stay for the company.

A Halloween-week paint night: settle in with a brush and a sip to create “Three Ghosts,” a seasonal canvas to take home. [tale title] The First Pinecone Bowling Championship

[tale] Loredas stayed dry all morning, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) declared the Hearth clearing open for the First Pinecone Bowling Championship. The pins were ten proud acorns in a row. The ball was the roundest pinecone in the forest. Henny (the Hearth’s chicken) kept score by clucking once for every pin down, which made her the busiest official in the Hold.

Earl (an elk) rolled first, with great dignity and no aim at all — his pinecone veered into Mabel’s herb basket and he declared it a practice throw. Then Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) breathed one careful ribbon of ice-mist down the lane to make it properly slick, and Jethro took his run-up just as the afternoon showers arrived.

That dang ol’ Jethro hit the slick lane at full trot, slid past the acorns, past Henny, and clean into the rain barrel, taking all ten pins down with the splash. Henny clucked ten times without stopping. The championship trophy — a shiny bottle cap from Flurry’s hoard — is still in the barrel, and Jethro says that is exactly where champions keep them.

[tale image caption] The championship roll — ten pins, one splash.

[tale title] The Great Pumpkin Weigh-In

[tale] Fredas dawned bright and clear, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) declared the First Great Pumpkin Weigh-In open before breakfast. His pumpkin — raised in Mabel’s compost corner and proud of it — sat on the Hearth’s scale like a small orange hill, while Mabel (a wood elf) read the tally board and sighed in an official capacity.

[tale title] The Great Kite Trial

[tale] Turdas dawned sunny with a brisk wind worrying the pines, and Gus (a friendly orc baker) decided his new diamond kite ought to be tested before lunch, not after. “Wind waits for no pie,” he said, which Mabel (a wood elf) noted was not a saying.

[tale] Middas dawned sunny and clear, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) declared the fallen leaves in the Hearth clearing wasted lying flat. [headline] Rain Soaks the Rim as Art, Music & Hula Fill the Week

[dateline] Monday, October 12, 2026

[lead] PAYSON — Hail, good neighbor, and mind the puddles! Morndas has thrown open the very floodgates over the Mogollon Rim, with rain drumming the pines all day and a Flood Watch standing till five o'clock — a fine day for the mead hall, the museum shelf, and watching Gandy glare at the sky from the dry boards. By the Nine, keep your cloak handy today and your dancing shoes ready for the weekend.

[hero_caption] The week ahead paints itself: ARToberFest in Payson, easels up across Sedona, and fall festivals under the Rim.

[weather] Rain — Flood Watch until 5 PM high 59 low 52 rain 80% (~0.5 in.) sunrise 6:28 AM sunset 5:54 PM tomorrow Morning rain, then partly cloudy, 59/44

[weather_caption] Gandy guards the dry boards while Maevy tries to catch the sky.

[weather_overheard] Overheard Last Night — A soaked traveler asked the barkeep when the rain would let up. The barkeep only shrugged: “Aye — the Watch runs till five, but the pines will believe it when they see it.”

[today Pine-Strawberry] Open Mic Night: Music with a Purpose — 4–7 PM at THAT Brewery & Pub, 3270 N AZ-87, Pine. The community open mic returns on its every-other-Monday rhythm, hosted this season by the Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction crew, with all tips going to forest-protection work. Seasoned pickers, first-time singers, poets, and storytellers all take the little stage — or just claim a pint and a bench and let the neighbors entertain you. A warm, wood-stove sort of evening; the rain on the roof only improves it.

[today Prescott] Prescott History Tour — 10 AM–noon, departing downtown Prescott. A two-hour guided walk through the old territorial capital's most storied streets, from Whiskey Row's saloons to the Victorian mansions of Nob Hill, led by guides who know every governor and ghost. Book ahead at freakyfoottours.com. A fine outing for history-curious guests — and the rain gives Whiskey Row a properly atmospheric gleam. | Fall Break Nature Camp — Monday through Friday, 8 AM–4 PM, Highlands Center for Natural History, 1375 S Walker Rd. A fully outdoor week of hiking, games, science investigations, and journaling on Prescott National Forest trails, for ages 6–10. $250 for members, $300 for non-members. (The Seedlings half-day track for little ones is full, with a waitlist.) | Fall Zoo Camp — Monday through Friday, 8:30 AM–3 PM, Heritage Park Zoological Sanctuary, 1403 Heritage Park Rd. Ages 6–12 get hands-on animal time, behind-the-scenes visits, wildlife games, crafts, and investigations at Prescott's hometown zoo. $250 for members, $300 for non-members. A grand week for young naturalists.

[week Tuesday, Oct. 13] Trail Day Volunteer Build — 7 AM–noon, off AZ-87 just before Pine. The Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction crew calls hikers, bikers, runners, and forest-lovers to clear brush, move rock, and shape new trail that doubles as firefighter access. No experience needed and tools are provided — bring water, gloves, and sturdy boots, and RSVP to trails@psfuelreduction.org for the meeting spot. Honest work under tall pines, and the best breakfast appetite you'll earn all week.

[week Thursday, Oct. 15] A Band Called Honalee — 7 PM, Payson High School Auditorium, 301 S McLane Rd. A modern folk trio channeling Peter, Paul & Mary — “Leaving on a Jet Plane,” “Blowin' in the Wind,” “Puff the Magic Dragon” — in close three-part harmony, with nods to Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and the Mamas & the Papas. Thirty-odd locals have already flagged they're going. A gentle, sing-along sort of evening for folk hearts. | Gary Allan with Julie Eddy — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, 3201 N Main St, Prescott Valley. The country hitmaker behind “Man to Man” and “Every Storm (Runs Out of Rain)” brings his raspy honky-tonk show to the region's big arena. The week's biggest-ticket concert — third-party listings show seats from about $64. A proper arena night out under the Rim.

[week Friday, Oct. 16] ARToberFest — Friday through Sunday, Mazatzal Casino Event Center. The Payson Art League's annual fine art and fine craft show and sale gathers the Hold's artists all in one hall, with the Payson Jazz Trio playing and an art raffle benefiting local school art programs. Come to browse or come to buy — the raffle alone is worth the trip, and the whole weekend hums. | 22nd Annual Sedona Plein Air Festival — Friday through Oct. 24, Sedona Arts Center, 15 Art Barn Rd, plus painting sites across Sedona and the Verde Valley. One of the West's oldest plein air festivals: dozens of master artists painting the red rocks outdoors, with free public demonstrations and paint-outs all week long. Free to watch the artists work; the grand sale closes the festival Oct. 24.

[week Saturday, Oct. 17] Fest of Fall — Saturday, Posse Grounds Park, 525 Posse Ground Rd (the city lists 11 AM–5 PM). Sedona's family fall celebration: food trucks, local brews, live music, craft and nonprofit vendors, pickleball and cornhole tournaments, a kids' zone with pumpkin carving, skate jam, and photo booth. Pair it with the morning's Pumpkin Splash at the community pool (11 AM–1 PM, $5 — pick your pumpkin right out of the water). Free, low-waste, and made for lingering. | 21st Annual Ho'ike — Hula Exhibition — Doors 12:30 PM, show 1 PM, Phillip England Center for the Performing Arts, 280 Camp Lincoln Rd, Camp Verde. Authentic Hawaiian hula, music, and culture in the Verde Valley: a scholar's presentation on ancient hula instruments opens the show, followed by modern hula, a 50-50 raffle, island goods, and a silent auction of Hawaiian art. Proceeds benefit Aloha 'Aina O Hawai'i. The most transporting afternoon of the week.

[week Sunday, Oct. 18] Howl-O-Ween Dog Costume Parade — 10 AM–noon (check-in 9–9:30 AM), Tlaquepaque Arts & Shopping Village, 336 SR-179, Sedona. The 6th annual parade of costumed canines, from Calle Independencia to Tlaquepaque North — $20 per dog, with proceeds to the Humane Society of Sedona. Costume contests carry $100 prizes (Doggone Cutest, Craziest Canine, and the group Leaders of the Pack), judged by the mayor-elect himself. Even dogless, it's the happiest two hours in the Verde Valley.

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] Twenty-five thousand square feet of treasure on the Beeline — antiques, fine art, and high-end jewelry, plus a glittering back wing of gems, rocks, and minerals that would make a dragon weep with envy. Native American artifacts, cowboy memorabilia, vintage books, taxidermy, and room after room of frontier curiosities. [tale title] The Great Trench Rescue

[tale] Morndas dawned with the sky wrung out over the Rim, and Mabel (a wood elf) stood in her herb garden watching her sage drown. “Trench,” she announced, the way a general declares war. “We dig a trench, or the thyme goes swimming.”

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took this as a personal commission. He dropped to all fours and plowed a furrow down the middle of the garden with his whole enormous body, humming a digging song, while Earl (an elk) stood by in enormous dignity holding Mabel's plumb line in his antlers so she could sight the slope. “Left,” said Mabel. Earl leaned left. “Right.” Earl leaned right, and the plumb bob swung round and bopped him square on the nose.

Gus (a friendly orc) arrived with a tray of trench pies — “morale rations,” he rumbled softly — just as Henny (a plump red-combed chicken) declared the deepest puddle her personal pond and christened it with a splash.

By noon the garden drained sweet as a whistle. The single casualty: Jethro's trench ran a touch too true and drained Mabel's rain barrel clean through the fence boards. Jethro stared at the empty barrel, then up at the weeping sky, and said, “Well. The sky will fill it back.”

Mabel sighed like it was her job. “It had better,” she said. “It's on trench duty next.”

[tale image caption] Jethro plows the trench while Earl sights the slope and Henny christens the puddles.

[headline] A Stormy Sundas: Quilts, Chili, and the Last Fair Day

[dateline] Sunday, October 11, 2026

[lead] PAYSON — Hail, travelers! Sundas dawned grey and growling over the Mogollon Rim, the storm drumming the pines while the Holds made merry indoors: today is the last day of the Rim Country Quilt Round-Up in Payson, the Fall & Antique Festival's chili cook-off in Pine, and Fort Verde Days' homecoming celebration down in Camp Verde. Keep an eye on the sky — a Flood Watch holds till Monday's small hours — and keep the week in your sights, for the days ahead bring trail-building, folk songs, the town council's gathering on Wednesday, and the Payson Art League's ARToberFest filling the weekend. By the Nine, there's no weather too wild for Rim Country doings.

[hero_caption] A market fair beneath the pines: quilts on the line, chili on the fire, and pumpkins by the antique stall.

[weather] Heavy thunderstorms — Flood Watch until Mon 5 AM; Wind Advisory 8 AM–8 PM high 61 low 54 rain 100% (~1.19 in.) sunrise 6:27 AM sunset 5:55 PM tomorrow Rain, 59/51

[weather_caption] Gandy keeps his grump dry under the eaves while Maevy conducts the rain.

[today Payson] Rim Country Quilt Round-Up — Last day today. The quilt guild's autumn gathering fills the Mazatzal Hotel & Casino Event Center with quilting classes and displays of fine stitchery — rows of finished quilts, demonstrations, and vendors for the fabric-minded. Wander the aisles for an hour or a day; quilters are the friendliest folk in the Hold. (Runs Friday through today, Sunday, Oct. 11.) | ACA Race #3 // Ubuntu Trail — The Arizona Cycling Association's scholastic mountain-bike series rolls into the Payson Event Center and Ubuntu Trail area today, with the first races off at 8 AM and awards late in the afternoon. Middle- and high-school racers from across the North Conference take on the course while families cheer from the sidelines. Come watch the future of Rim Country riding.

[today Pine-Strawberry] Annual Fall & Antique Festival — Last day today, 9 AM–4 PM at the Pine-Strawberry Community Center, 3886 N Hwy 87 in Pine. A chili cook-off, food and craft vendors, a pumpkin patch, and an antique show inside the Cultural Hall — the twin villages' autumn send-off in one stop. Come hungry; leave with something old. (Runs Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10–11.)

[today Camp Verde] Fort Verde Days — Last day today of Camp Verde's big annual homecoming, the town's celebration of the frontier military post it grew up around. Sunday brings vendors, entertainment, and living-history events at Fort Verde State Historic Park, 646 S. 1st Street — admission free. Saturday's parade has passed, but the old camp's story carries the day. (Runs Friday through Sunday, Oct. 9–11.)

[today Sedona] Sedona Community Farmers Market — Sundays, now on winter hours: 11 AM–3 PM at the Wells Fargo parking lot, 2201 W SR 89A, weekly through May 30, 2027. Local growers, bakers, and makers set out their tables for the valley's regular Sunday trade. Worth the drive for the fresh bread alone. | Alternative Firing 1-Day Workshop with CJ Henderson — 10 AM at 15 Art Barn Rd. A hands-on day of pottery finishing techniques — raku-style alternative firings that coax fire-born color from the clay. All skill levels welcome; take home something the kiln gods smiled on.

[today Prescott] Prescott History Tour — 10 AM. A two-hour guided walk through downtown Prescott with guides who know the streets and the folk who shaped them. Territorial capital tales, Whiskey Row lore, and the buildings that outlived them all. | Flashback — LIVE at Whiskey River Tavern — 1 PM at 214 S. Montezuma St. A retro and classic cover band keeps the afternoon singing and dancing. Come for the sing-along crowd; bring your best air guitar. | La Posada – Stage to Screen — 3 PM at the Prescott Elks Theater, 117 E Gurley St. Missed the stage production? See it on screen with archival photographs tracing the history. A quiet, lovely way to spend a stormy afternoon.

[week Monday, Oct. 12] Open Mic Night: Music with a Purpose — 4 PM at THAT Brewery & Pub, 3270 N Hwy 87, Pine. The community open mic in the pines where every donation gives back locally. Bring an instrument or just your voice; the forest provides the acoustics. | Mud Run, Schnebly Hill — Noon start at the bottom of Schnebly Hill near Sedona. [week Tuesday, Oct. 13] Trail Day Volunteer Build — 7 AM at Hwy 87, Pine. Pine-Strawberry Fuel Reduction calls hikers, bikers, and runners to build trail — "don't just use the trail, help build it." Gloves, water, and stout boots; breakfast of champions optional but recommended.

[week Thursday, Oct. 15] A Band Called Honalee — 7 PM, Payson High School Auditorium, 301 S. McLane Rd. A folk trio reliving Peter, Paul & Mary — "Leaving on a Jet Plane," "Blowin' in the Wind," "Puff the Magic Dragon" — plus Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and the Mamas & the Papas. An evening of harmony under the auditorium lights. | Gary Allan — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, 3201 N. Main Street, Prescott Valley. The country headliner takes the stage with a special guest. Tickets moving; worth the drive down the mountain for the faithful.

[week Friday, Oct. 16] 3rd Friday Art Walk — 4–6 PM on Main Street, Camp Verde. Galleries and shops open their doors for a free evening stroll. Meet the makers, sip something warm, and watch the street turn gallery. | ARToberFest — Friday through Sunday at the Mazatzal Casino Event Center. The Payson Art League's annual fine art and fine craft show and sale, with the Payson Jazz Trio and an art raffle benefiting local school art programs. The Hold's artists, all in one hall.

[merchant town] Payson

[tale title] The Pie-Dish Regatta

[tale] The storm had turned the Hearth's clearing into a lake, and Gus (a friendly orc with a baker's soul) was having thoughts.

"The pond reaches the porch," he announced, holding his warmest apple pie over his head, "and my pies must reach the porch people. So the pies must sail."

Before Mabel (a wood elf) could finish saying "Gus, no—", he had launched his biggest copper pie dish onto the flood like a raft and climbed aboard, pie held aloft.

Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon), delighted, seized the tow rope in his claws and flapped skyward — which, with his kinked tail, meant a zigzag course straight at the porch, then away from it, then sideways.

"Port! Starboard! No, the OTHER port!" shouted Mabel from the dry porch, waving her arms like a harbormaster.

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) waded in cheering, and Henny (the Hearth's plump Skyrim-style chicken) perched on the dish's rim like a figurehead, serene as a duchess.

Earl (an elk), dignified and dry beneath the pines, declined to participate. The sky declined to notice. One Flurry loop later, a wave crested the pie dish and crowned Earl's antlers — and the only dry thing in the clearing was the pie, which Gus delivered to the porch without spilling a crumb.

[tale image caption] Gus sails his pie-dish raft across the flooded clearing, Flurry at the tow rope.

[headline] Thunder on the Rim: The Big Show Rolls Into Green Valley Park

[dateline] Saturday, October 10, 2026

[lead] Hail, traveler, and lend the morning sky your ear — the Rim wakes with thunder in its throat and a grand day in its parks. PAYSON — the thirty-third Beeline Cruise-In Classic Car Show rolls into Green Valley Park this morning, classics and rat rods on the grass from 8 AM to 3 PM, with the town's own Payson Days celebration — live music, vendors, and fireworks — to close the night, storms permitting. Camp Verde answers with drum and cannon for the seventieth Fort Verde Days, Sedona crams an arts festival, a blues festival, and warbirds into a single Saturday, and the school mountain-bike championships race the rain. Read on — and mind the flood watch: it runs from 11 AM through Monday morning.

[hero_caption] The thirty-third Beeline Cruise-In turns Green Valley Park into a fair of gleaming horse-drawn caravans — storm clouds be damned.

[weather] Isolated thunderstorms high 72 low 58 rain 30% day, 90% night sunrise 6:27 AM sunset 5:57 PM tomorrow Thunderstorms, 62/54

[weather_caption] Gandy flat-out refuses the storm; Maevy conducts the rain on the railing.

[weather_overheard] Overheard Last Night — A soaked traveler asked the barkeep whether the Dragonborn could not simply shout the storm aside. The barkeep only shrugged: “Aye — he shouted this morning. The thunder was just answering back.”

[today Payson] 33rd Annual Beeline Cruise-In Classic Car Show — 8 AM–3 PM, Green Valley Park, 600 S Green Valley Pkwy. The Beeline Cruisers Motor Club's thirty-third annual show: classic cars, trucks, lowriders, and rat rods — every one 25 years or older — lined up on the park grass for Best of Show and a wagon-load of category awards. Food vendors, entertainment, and raffles raising money for local charities, all free to the public. (The Friday pre-show cruise through central Payson already rolled yesterday afternoon.) | Payson Days Celebration — follows the car show at Green Valley Park. The town's own annual celebration keeps the fair going with live performances, a variety of food and vendor booths, and a fireworks display to close the night — storms permitting. Free admission, and the whole Hold comes out for it. | ACA Race #3 — Ubuntu Trail — Payson Event Center. The Arizona Cycling Association's interscholastic mountain-bike series hits the purpose-built singletrack: middle and high school riders from across the state, all in one stormy day. The organizer moved both conferences' racing to Saturday in short-track format (roughly 8 AM–3 PM, awards at 3) — Sunday racing is off.

[today Camp Verde] 70th Annual Fort Verde Days — Parade steps off at 10 AM down Main Street (finishing at the General Crook turnoff), this year's theme “America 250” with Grand Marshal Bob Weir. The festival on the town grounds at Main & Hollamon runs 11 AM–7 PM: food and craft vendors, live music, and contests. At Fort Verde State Historic Park: flag-raising and -lowering ceremonies, artillery demonstrations, living-history reenactors, Dutch-oven cooking, and military drills — free park admission all weekend. | Verde Valley Archaeology Center Indigenous Peoples Day Celebration — 10 AM–4 PM, 460 W. Finnie Flat Road. A free-admission day honoring Native American heritage: a Native American Artist Market with 30+ artists (fine art, weaving, pottery, jewelry, katsinas, silversmith work, apparel, crafts), homemade fry bread for purchase, and a noon talk by master Zuni carver Clive J. Hustito on Zuni fetishes — their symbolism and meaning — with a complimentary reception after. Note: the parade briefly closes part of Finnie Flat Road; the museum stays reachable through the Bashas' plaza entrance.

[today Sedona] 35th Annual Sedona Arts Festival — 9 AM–5 PM, Sedona Red Rock High School, 995 Upper Red Rock Loop Rd. Sedona's oldest and largest fine-arts event: 100+ juried artists from across the country showing glass, painting, metal, woodworking, photography, and ceramics, plus live music, food trucks, a beer & wine garden, and a Gourmet Row of locally made kitchen and home goods. A $15 pass covers both days; children 12 and under free with a paying adult. | Sedona Airport Wings & Wheels 2026 — 9 AM–4 PM at the Sedona Airport (up Airport Road to Tabletop Mesa). Classic cars meet classic aircraft: T-34s, T-28s, F-35 formation flybys after lunchtime, a simulated fire water drop, and the centerpiece Consolidated PB4Y-2 “Privateer” — the world's only airworthy one. Admission is a $2 donation or a nonperishable food item, every bit of it going to the Sedona Community Food Bank. | 6th Annual Sedona Red Rockin' Blues Festival — gates 11:30 AM, show noon–5 PM, Posse Grounds Pavilion, 525 Posse Ground Rd. The Northern Arizona Blues Alliance serves up local and regional Arizona blues talent — nearly all Arizona Blues Hall of Fame inductees — on the grass under the red rocks. $25 wristbands at the gate (cash only) cover the whole day of come-and-go; bring folding chairs, coolers (no alcohol), and sunblock; leashed dogs welcome.

[today Prescott] Prescott Antique Show & Vintage Market — 8 AM–3 PM, Prescott Rodeo Grounds, 840 Rodeo Dr. 50+ antique dealers from Arizona and the surrounding states: Western collectibles, Victorian antiques, mid-century furniture, vintage toys, and Native American jewelry. $10 general admission; every cent of proceeds goes to historic preservation, restoration, and education. Presented by the Thumb Butte & Yavapai Questers. | R.O.C.K. in the USA — The Music of John Mellencamp — 7:00–9:30 PM, Prescott Elks Theater, 117 E Gurley St. A high-energy tribute to Rock & Roll Hall of Famer John Mellencamp's five decades of heartland rock hits — the small-town anthems that practically wrote themselves for this Hold. Tickets run about $41–53. | Music on the Green — 4–7 PM, Prescott Valley. A free outdoor concert under the open sky with The Offbeats, a high-energy punk rock cover band tearing through Foo Fighters, Paramore, and Audioslave. Pack a blanket, grab the Valley Dwellers, and close out the afternoon loud.

[week Sun, Oct. 11] 70th Annual Fort Verde Days — day two in Camp Verde. The festival grounds at Main & Hollamon run 11 AM–4 PM, and Fort Verde State Historic Park keeps free admission 10 AM–4 PM — flag ceremonies, reenactors, and Dutch-oven demos. The Little Britches and Little Petticoats frontier-costume contest parades the littlest ones at 11 AM in the Seating Tent. | 35th Annual Sedona Arts Festival — day two, 10 AM–4 PM at Sedona Red Rock High School. Your $15 Saturday pass covers Sunday too: 100+ juried artists, live music, food trucks, and the beer & wine garden, all with the red rocks standing watch.

[week Wed, Oct. 14] Payson Town Council — regular meeting 4:00 PM in the Town Council Chambers at Town Hall, 303 N Beeline Hwy. Agendas post at least 24 hours ahead, so headline items should appear around Oct. 13 on the town's meetings page. Meetings also stream live on the town's YouTube channel. | Willow Lake Guided Walk & Open House — Prescott. A 3 PM easy walk around the south side of Willow Lake with wildlife expert Walt Anderson and butterfly enthusiast Becky Hardy (sturdy shoes, dress in layers), followed by the Willow Lake Community Open House 4–6 PM at the Phippen Museum — displays and city staff on hand, drop in anytime.

[week Thu, Oct. 15] Gary Allan — 7:30 PM, Findlay Toyota Center, 3201 N Main St, Prescott Valley. The country star brings his arena show to the Hold on a tour stop between Tacoma and Chandler. Tickets through Ticketmaster.

[merchant name] Kendra's Country Bakery

[merchant town] Payson

[merchant blurb] A homegrown bakehouse on the Beeline turning out made-from-scratch cakes, cupcakes, cookies, and their famous bubble waffles. Kendra and Maureen are the edible-art duo behind some of Rim Country's most talked-about wedding cakes. The little storefront smells like butter and vanilla from the sidewalk.

[merchant review] Everything is delicious, best bubble waffles in the world!

[merchant review_src] a Restaurantji review

[tale title] The Storm-Welcome Service

[tale] With thunderstorms rumbling off the Rim, Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) declared the Hold's guests deserved a proper stormy-day greeting. So he set up his welcome station on the Hearth's front deck with a bundle of pine-bough parasols he'd lashed together himself.

The idea was sound. The parasols — being pine boughs — were enormous, fragrant, and utterly at the mercy of the wind. Every gust snatched one clean out of Jethro's hands and sent it cartwheeling across the deck. Henny the chicken took cover under the eaves and clucked advice nobody asked for.

Earl the elk, ever dignified, volunteered to hold the welcome banner in his antlers so it wouldn't blow away. But every gust caught the banner's loose end and slapped it smartly across Earl's muzzle, and each time he bowed a little deeper — as though saying, “you're welcome.”

Finally Mabel the wood elf herded the whole soaked crew inside for warm bread and cider, sighing like it was her job — which, in this forest, it is. “Best welcome ever,” the dripping guests declared. Jethro beamed. “Same time next storm?”

[tale title] The Great Sage Freeze

[tale] Mabel (a wood elf) had a plan: winter is coming, her sage must be dried, and Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) is the Hold’s walking icebox. So on a drizzly morning she enlisted him to freeze-dry the whole harvest — a slow, careful breath, no zigzags, no funny business.

Flurry drew himself up tall, took aim at the sage bundles hanging from her garden trellis, and breathed out the steadiest, proudest ice-mist of his young life. The sage froze to perfection, glittering like diamonds on a Nord shield.

That was when Henny (the Hearth’s chicken), mid-beetle-chase, skidded through the garden at full waddle and slid, feathers and all, across the wet grass — straight into Flurry’s ice-mist. She emerged glazed like a pastry, froze mid-step, and then, unbothered professional that she is, caught her reflection in a frozen puddle and began to preen.

Mabel sighed the sigh of the only responsible adult in the forest. Gus, arriving with an empty pie dish, took one look, broke off a leaf of ice-sage, tasted it, and declared it “minty.”

The Hold’s first frost-dried herbs. Mabel calls it a disaster. The mead hall calls it seasoning.

[tale] That dang ol’ Jethro was at it again Monday morning, convinced the Hearth’s front door lacked a proper greeting. It wasn’t. The breeze coming off the pines struck up a racket like a marching band falling down a staircase, and Earl (the elk) planted himself under the sign with his great antlers tilted back, suffering in silence the way only Earl can.

Then Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) — perched on the signpost to watch the chaos — let out a tremendous sneeze, and a fine ice-mist glazed every pan. The next gust struck the frosted pans and they rang out clear and sweet as temple bells.

[tale title] The Sunbeam Coronation

[tale] Earl (an elk with enormous antlers) takes his dignity seriously, and this fine sunny morning he took it straight to the Hearth’s front deck, where one perfect sunbeam lay across the planks like a warm rug. He lowered himself into it with great ceremony, folded his legs, and announced that he would be napping, and was not to be disturbed.

Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took this as an invitation to help. He fetched a pine bough to fan the great napping elk — “for the flies,” he said proudly — and waved it so enthusiastically that the first pine cone dropped straight onto Earl’s nose.

Earl did not move. Dignity, he has always maintained, is staying put.

The second cone bounced off one antler. The third landed in the crook of the other and stayed there, like a small brown crown.

Mabel (a wood elf) came out with the washing, took one look, and said what everyone was thinking: “Well. It suits him.”

Earl opened one eye, considered the crown, and went back to sleep. Some nappers get pine needles. Earl got a coronation.

[tale] It rained on Middas afternoon, the soft gray kind, and Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) took it as a personal invitation.  Nobody’s quite sure whose idea it was — Henny (the Hearth’s plump chicken) claims she only mentioned the rain looked “a mite plain” — but by mid-afternoon Flurry was perched on the Hearth’s front deck, exhaling his finest ice-mist into the drizzle, gilding every falling drop into a tiny glittering jewel.  “I am gilding the rain,” he announced grandly, then landed sideways in a rain barrel for emphasis.  By the time Gus (a friendly orc with a baker’s soul) came out with a tray of honey cakes, the whole deck sparkled like a kicked-over treasure chest. He took one step, skidded clean across the jewel-ice, and landed sitting down with the tray held high overhead — not one crumb lost.  “Save the cakes!” he bellowed, which is how Gus says “I’m fine.”  Mabel (a wood elf with the patience of a saint) surveyed the glittering deck, the dragon in the rain barrel, and the orc on his backside, and declared Flurry the Hold’s first official weathermage. [tale title] Earl’s Laundry Service

[tale] The sun came out grand on Turdas morning, and Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) took one look at his dripping wash line and had what he called a notion.

“Earl,” he announced, “you’re the tallest rack in the Hold.”

Earl (an elk with enormous antlers) stood very still, which everyone took for agreement. By mid-morning his antlers wore two shirts, a row of socks, and one magnificent sheet billowing like a sail bound for Scotland, that mist-shrouded realm across the eastern sea.

[tale] On a blazing Loredas morning, the kind of bright where the shadows themselves squinted, Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) announced that Flurry needed landing lessons.

Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) flies in a fine straight line, Jethro explained, which is the easy part. The hard part is the arriving. Ever since the rain-barrel incident his tail has had a kink, so he flies in zigzags and lands wherever the wind argues him into — last week that was Gus the orc baker's pie-cooling rack, and the week before, Mabel's herb bed, which is still not over it.

So Jethro laid out a landing strip of pine needles in the sunny clearing, planted two tiny signal flags, and waved Flurry in. Earl (an elk) stood by as the tower, enormous antlers held high, calling the altitude in his most official voice. "Two tail-lengths! One! Flare!"

Flurry flared. Flurry zigged. Flurry zagged — and set down neat as you please in the middle of the strip, wings folded, looking enormously pleased with himself.

Jethro wept with pride. Earl logged it in the bark ledger: one good landing. Then the wind shifted, and Flurry's victory lap ended in Gus's pie rack again.

One out of two, the forest agreed, is a personal best.

[tale title] The Guest Book

[tale] Sundas dawned warm as a fresh honey-cake, and the road past the Hearth filled with faire-folk and Valley Dwellers trading the lowland heat for Rim Country air — which put Jethro (the Mogollon Monster) in a welcoming frame of mind.

“The Hearth needs a guest book,” he announced, and dragged a hollow log up to the front door.

Being a monster of few letters, Jethro's guest book required no writing: each traveler dropped one shiny thing into the log. Flurry (a young ice-breathing dragon) appointed himself curator, rejecting three pinecones and a lost button before Mabel (a wood elf) ruled that sentiment counted.

Henny (the Hearth's plump Skyrim-style chicken) inspected each offering for edibility, and found them all wanting.

When a little girl dropped in a bottle cap polished to mirror-bright, Jethro was so moved he tried to hug the whole log — and tipped it clean over. Forty-seven shinies rolled down the sunlit deck in every direction. Flurry zigzagged after them on his kinked tail, collecting them twice as fast as they rolled, while Earl (an elk) stood very still in the middle of it all, dignity intact, pretending with great success that nothing was happening.

Mabel righted the log, declared it a guest log in the most literal sense, and Gus (an orc baker) arrived with honey-cakes — which Jethro entered into the book the only way he knew how: he drew a picture of a chicken judging a pinecone.
